title: Daily Doctrine

items.title: Theology
items.summary: Christian theology is not cold information about God but the pursuit of seeing his glory in Christ so we can love him, enjoy him, and follow him. Studying God should be grounded in Scripture as the final test, use the mind as a servant of faith rather than its master, and be marked by dependence and teachability instead of pride. The payoff is doxology: clearer thinking should deepen worship, not replace it. When doctrine stays tethered to the Bible and humbly received, it becomes the path to a richer walk with the Lord we were made to know.

items.title: Systematic Theology
items.summary: Systematic theology asks what the entire Bible teaches about a given topic—sin, grace, Christ, the Spirit, the church, and the rest—and arranges those answers in an orderly way. It sits alongside other disciplines like tracing themes through Scripture or studying how doctrine developed in history, but its distinctive work is topical and logical. Classic outlines often move from Scripture and method through God, humanity, Christ, salvation, the church, and last things. The point is not minimum knowledge for heaven but a fuller portrait of God’s character and works, moving from vague slogans to careful, worship-shaping truth.

items.title: Divisions of Theology
items.summary: Reformed thinkers, especially Franciscus Junius, sorted theology into helpful categories. False theology rests on human opinion alone; true theology begins with God’s own perfect self-knowledge, then the copy of that knowledge he graciously gives creatures. Christ knows God in a unique way; glorified saints know differently from pilgrims on earth. Some truth comes through creation and conscience, but after the fall that path is partial and cannot redeem. Supernatural revelation in Scripture is what sinners must hear to be saved, and that revealed theology is what systematic study mainly examines.

items.title: Religion
items.summary: Today many treat “religion” as the enemy of grace—empty ritual or merit-earning—but Scripture and church history use the word more neutrally and often positively. Biblical religion can be corrupt when self-made or hypocritical, yet James praises religion that cares for the vulnerable and keeps the heart pure. Jesus attended synagogue, upheld moral instruction, instituted baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and built a disciplined community. Rejecting religion wholesale can unintentionally reject the structured, doctrinal, communal life the gospel actually establishes.

items.title: Science
items.summary: Calling theology a “science” does not reduce the Bible to a lab specimen. Reformed teachers like Charles Hodge meant that Christian doctrine should treat Scripture as a reliable storehouse of facts and arrange those facts into a coherent, noncontradictory whole—much as natural science orders observations about the world. Medieval and post-Reformation debates used older categories of knowledge to ask whether theology counts as rigorous knowledge of truth. The consensus among classic Reformed dogmaticians is yes: theology pursues dependable knowledge of God through careful induction from what God has said.

items.title: Speculative or Practical?
items.summary: Theology must never stay abstract in a way that never reaches the heart and hands, yet it is not only a how-to manual. Aquinas stressed contemplation of God as the soul’s end; Turretin argued for a mixed science—truth worth knowing for its own sake and truth that must produce love and obedience. A sermon with no bullet-point application can still transform lives if it unveils Christ. Making theology purely “practical” has often been a tactic to sideline the Trinity, the incarnation, and other central mysteries. Faithful teaching holds knowing and doing together.

items.title: Ad Fontes
items.summary: The Reformation slogan “to the sources” called scholars and pastors back from layers of commentary to original texts—especially Scripture in its languages, and also the classics of antiquity. Renaissance humanism, distinct from modern secular versions, prized grammar, rhetoric, history, and moral instruction drawn from primary authors rather than endless scholastic debate. That movement had weaknesses when usefulness trumped truth, yet it prepared the way for Reformers who read the Bible closely, educated ordinary believers, and built churches where word-centered study and heartfelt piety belonged together.

items.title: Principia
items.summary: Reformed scholastics spoke of first principles in three senses: what makes something real, what lies outside us as the source of knowledge, and what inside us grasps that knowledge. For everyday sciences God is the ultimate ground of reality; creation is the external textbook; reason is the internal faculty. In theology God remains the foundation of all being and knowing, Holy Scripture is the external authority that interprets everything else, and faith—not bare speculation or private feeling—is how we receive what God says about himself and respond with trust and obedience.

items.title: Faith and Reason
items.summary: Faith and reason are allies when each keeps its place. Human judgment does not sit above God’s word to veto what seems impossible; reason instead helps us understand, organize, and defend what Scripture teaches. Drawing necessary conclusions from biblical premises is legitimate, as is rejecting contradictions. Faith does not bypass the mind, and the mind cannot generate the gospel on its own. Philosophy, used carefully, may supply categories and expose unbelieving inconsistency, but it must remain a helper to revelation, not a replacement for it.

items.title: Inner Testimony of the Holy Spirit
items.summary: Historical and textual arguments for the Bible have value, but the deepest reason Christians submit to Scripture is that the same Spirit who inspired the writers also persuades believers that these are God’s own words. Calvin warned against trying to establish trust in the Bible only by debate, as if human proofs came first. The Spirit’s work is not new revelation, a mere emotional boost, or the final ground of faith; it is how God opens blind eyes so we hear his voice in the written word and rest on Christ, not on our experience.

items.title: Fundamental Articles
items.summary: Christians agree that some doctrines are nonnegotiable while others allow conscientious disagreement, but drawing the line takes wisdom. Calvin noted that not every truth carries equal weight: some are basic pillars everyone should hold, others are important yet not church-dividing. After the Reformation, Catholics, Socinians, and Protestants debated how much unity required. Helpful distinctions separate errors that destroy saving faith from those that weaken maturity, and creeds like Nicene give a historical floor, not a ceiling. Paul’s gospel pattern—holy God, guilty sinners, crucified and risen Christ, grace through faith unto holiness—sets the minimum faithful summary.

items.title: Knowing God
items.summary: The living God wants to be known, but only on his terms. Rationalism treats human reason as the highest court and often shrinks the supernatural to fit current fashions. Mysticism seeks private impressions apart from the written word, confusing illumination with new messages. Liberalism makes modern experience the judge of doctrine. Historic Christianity insists that God speaks objectively from outside us; our minds and the Spirit’s help are real, but both serve Scripture rather than replacing it. True knowledge balances humble limits with eager attention to what God has plainly revealed.

items.title: Natural Law and Natural Theology
items.summary: God has written a moral order on the human conscience and displayed his power and deity in the world he made. Natural law names the standards of right and wrong all people sense; natural theology names what reason can infer about the Creator from creation, human nature, and providence. Paul and the psalmists assume even unbelievers are without excuse. Yet this universal witness is dim, easily suppressed, and cannot tell sinners how to be forgiven. Major voices from Augustine through the Reformers, Westminster, and Old Princeton affirmed natural knowledge while insisting that saving knowledge comes only through the gospel in Scripture.

items.title: General Revelation and Special Revelation
items.summary: God makes himself known broadly through the heavens, history, and conscience—what confessions call the light of nature—so that no one can plead total ignorance. That general disclosure shows God as powerful Creator and moral Judge but not as Redeemer. Sinners need special revelation: God’s saving will spoken finally and fully in the written Scriptures. We therefore speak of a twofold knowledge—God as Maker through creation, God as Savior through his word. Science can explore an orderly world that points to its Maker, yet it cannot answer questions about forgiveness and eternal life where only Scripture speaks with clarity and authority.

items.title: Inspiration
items.summary: Scripture is God’s exhaled speech: every part, not only devotional sections, carries divine authority because the Spirit moved human authors. Paul’s letters and Peter’s recognition of Paul show the New Testament writings standing alongside the Old as God’s word. Inspiration is a finished fact about the text, not a feeling readers generate in the moment. The Bible does not merely contain God’s message in spots where we encounter him; the written words themselves are his message. God breathed out Scripture so that through teaching, correction, and training believers would be equipped—and ultimately drawn to worship the Christ the text reveals.

items.title: Concursive Operation
items.summary: Explaining how God produced Scripture avoids two errors. A loose “dynamic” view treats biblical writers like unusually inspired poets whose words may err. Mechanical dictation imagines authors as passive stenographers, a picture closer to other religions than to Christianity. The biblical picture is concursive: the Spirit carried prophets and apostles along so that their personalities, vocabularies, and research remained genuinely theirs while the result was still entirely God’s truthful speech. Human agency and divine authority interwoven—like wind filling a sail—yield a book that is truly human in form and flawlessly divine in message.

items.title: Perfections of Scripture
items.summary: Four classic attributes, often remembered as SCAN, describe how Christians relate to the Bible. Sufficiency means Scripture tells us everything necessary for salvation and the Christian life because Christ’s finished work and apostolic explanation are complete. Clarity means the main message can be understood by ordinary believers who study prayerfully, even if some details remain hard. Authority means the Spirit speaking in Scripture is the final court of appeal, not tradition, science, or personal opinion—sola Scriptura. Necessity means that after the apostles, the written word is indispensable; the church rests on their testimony, not on ongoing private revelations.

items.title: Inerrancy
items.summary: If God carried writers along so that their words were his, then Scripture cannot affirm what is false any more than God can lie. Jesus treated even small details and obscure texts as binding, coming from the Creator himself. Inerrancy is not a hobby horse of modern fundamentalism; Calvin and the wider tradition demanded reverent acceptance of all Scripture teaches. Denying full trustworthiness either splits God’s word from God or impugns his character. The issue is posture: believers live under the text, never editing divine speech to suit fashion. Embracing the Bible’s complete reliability guards both truth and spiritual vitality.

items.title: The Question of Canon
items.summary: Christians receive sixty-six books as the closed rule of faith: thirty-nine Old Testament writings recognized by Jesus and the apostles, plus twenty-seven New Testament documents rooted in apostolic authority. Old Testament boundaries were largely settled before late rabbinic gatherings; apocryphal works circulated in Greek but were treated as secondary by Jerome and Jewish tradition. The New Testament collection grew as churches heard the Lord’s authorized messengers; lists from early centuries show debate at the edges but steady agreement on the core. Councils in the fourth and fifth centuries formalized what believers already treasured. Revelation’s warning against adding or removing fits a covenant document sealing the storyline from Genesis onward.

items.title: Which Books Belong in the Bible?
items.summary: Canon formation was historical, yet the church did not invent authority by vote. Saying believers needed an infallible institution to pick books reverses the biblical pattern: God’s word creates and defines his people, from Abraham to the apostles. Catholic critics note Protestants lack an inspired table of contents, but self-authentication better matches how Israel received the Law and how early Christians recognized Gospels and epistles as bearing the apostles’ unique stamp. The community discerned what already rang with divine authority—like a child spotting parents in a crowd—not manufacturing Scripture from a menu of options.

items.title: The Existence of God
items.summary: Scripture opens with God present, not with a neutral universe waiting for proof. Every heart carries an awareness that leaves unbelievers accountable, and only folly denies the obvious. That starting point does not forbid thoughtful arguments; Aquinas and later Protestants offered ways of showing that motion, causation, design, conscience, and universal religious longing point to one necessary, intelligent Creator. Such reasoning should support revelation, not replace faith. Believing God exists remains a gift of faith, yet showing theism’s coherence can remove excuses and strengthen believers who defend the faith in a skeptical age.

items.title: The Knowability of God
items.summary: When we ask what God is like, we must admit both mystery and real knowledge. Isaiah and Job remind us that the Creator cannot be fully mapped by creatures; our vision here is partial. Yet “incomprehensible” does not mean “unknowable.” Deuteronomy distinguishes secret things belonging to the Lord from what he has disclosed for our obedience and joy. Jesus defined eternal life as knowing the Father and the Son. Humility refuses to shrink God to our categories, but it also refuses to ignore what he has spoken. Sound doctrine honors both the limits of human minds and the clarity of divine self-revelation.

items.title: Words for God
items.summary: Human language about God cannot work exactly like talk about everyday objects. If our words meant the same thing for God and creatures, we would treat the infinite as just another item in creation. If they meant entirely different things, we could say nothing true about him at all. The classic answer is analogical speech: terms such as good, wise, or loving point to real correspondence between Creator and image-bearers while acknowledging an infinite gap. Because humans reflect God’s image and creation displays his attributes, our words can genuinely describe the Lord even though he always exceeds what language can capture.

items.title: The Unity of God
items.summary: Monotheism is the bedrock of biblical faith: the Lord alone is God, indivisible in his being and without peer among supposed deities. Israel’s creed and the first commandment demand exclusive loyalty to one supreme ruler. Unity here means God’s essence cannot be chopped into parts, and also that no rival shares his infinite perfection. That truth fits with later revelation of Father, Son, and Spirit without splitting God into three beings. From Moses to the epistles, Scripture insists the universe is ruled by one great King, not chaos without a lord or a pantheon of equals.

items.title: The Spirituality of God
items.summary: Jesus told the Samaritan woman that God is spirit, meaning worship is not tied to a mountain or temple but to truth and the heart. Spirituality includes being nonphysical—no body to see—but goes further: God is pure spirit, eternal and invisible, not limited by space or time like creatures. He is not an abstract idea or impersonal force but a real substance with self-awareness and free will. Personality in God means he knows himself, chooses purposes, and relates personally to us. Later Trinitarian teaching shows how one divine nature exists in three persons who eternally know and love one another.

items.title: The Names of God
items.summary: Biblical names reveal character, not merely labels. Scholars group God’s titles into proper, essential, and personal categories; here the focus is proper names. Old Testament designations such as El, Elohim, Adonai, and El-Shaddai highlight power and rule, while Yahweh—the covenant name unveiled to Moses—stresses self-existence and faithful presence with his people. New Testament believers call him Theos, Kyrios, and especially Father, showing relationship though Scripture names him with masculine titles, not because God is male but because those names fit how he reveals his authority and care. Each name invites trust in the God who keeps his word.

items.title: The Attributes of God
items.summary: When we describe who God is, we speak of his attributes—the qualities that belong to him alone. These are not add-ons or parts stacked onto something else; whatever is true of God is true of his very being. Historic confessions and careful theologians have named him eternal, spirit, unchanging, all-powerful, wise, holy, and overflowing goodness. Such language can feel abstract, yet it guards the God we meet in Scripture from being shrunk to a mere character in stories. Naming God's perfections helps the church think clearly about his nature and worship him with greater reverence and joy.

items.title: Incommunicable and Communicable Attributes
items.summary: Theologians often sort God's qualities into two groups. Some traits belong to God alone in their full sense—limitlessness, eternity, and unchangeableness cannot be copied by creatures. Others, such as love, mercy, and goodness, have a real echo in human life, though always in a dependent and partial way. No list is perfect; even "shared" traits are only analogous to how we experience them. Still, the distinction helps us marvel at God's otherness while also seeing how his moral beauty can be reflected, however faintly, in those made in his image.

items.title: Substance and Accidents
items.summary: Classical philosophy distinguishes what a thing is in itself from the changeable features that describe it. A dog stays a dog whether it is spotted or brown; color is incidental to dog-ness. God is not built that way. He is not a simple subject carrying optional extras. Reformed teachers insisted that nothing true of God could be stripped away and leave "God" behind. His wisdom, power, and holiness are not detachable properties but identical with who he is. For the Creator, everything is essential; nothing about him is merely accidental.

items.title: Christian Theology and Greco-Roman Philosophy
items.summary: Scripture must always lead, yet Christian doctrine has long used philosophical terms to state biblical truth with precision. Western thought is soaked in categories like substance, nature, and person; avoiding them entirely is nearly impossible if we want to read the church's creeds intelligently. Those tools helped early believers hold together truths such as one God and three persons, or the full deity of the Son. The New Testament itself uses language that overlaps with contemporary metaphysics. Used wisely, such vocabulary serves the gospel rather than replacing it.

items.title: The Simplicity of God
items.summary: Divine simplicity means God is not assembled from ingredients or percentages of traits. He is not love plus power plus justice mixed into one being, nor is love somehow more "central" than holiness or sovereignty. Every scriptural declaration about what God is carries equal weight metaphysically: he is love, light, spirit, and holy fire without contradiction. Attributes do not cling to him like attachments; he is what his perfections are. Simplicity protects us from ranking God's character and reminds us that the one true God is utterly unlike every creature category we know.

items.title: Aseity
items.summary: Aseity teaches that God exists from himself and needs nothing outside himself to be God. The Bible opens with no backstory of gods fighting or raw matter waiting to be shaped—only the Lord who already is. Before creation's first moment, he was complete, self-sufficient, and free from loneliness or lack. All life, including ours, depends on him; he does not depend on the world. In a culture obsessed with self-discovery and self-creation, this truth anchors worship: only the triune God possesses life in himself and owes his being to no one.

items.title: Divine Infinity
items.summary: God's infinity can be considered in three directions. Toward himself, he is absolutely perfect—every attribute possessed without limit or deficiency. Toward time, he is eternal: no beginning, no end, no succession of before and after as creatures experience. Toward space, he is immense— not squeezed into temples or corners of the universe, yet present everywhere in his providence. Omnipresence highlights nearness; immensity highlights that nothing can contain him. Though we are finite, we are invited to know and praise the God whose being and rule have no boundary.

items.title: Immutability
items.summary: To say God is immutable is to confess that he cannot improve, decline, or shift in his essential nature. Change would imply room to become better or worse, but God is already maximal perfection. His name speaks pure being, not becoming. Promises hold because his character cannot swerve; plans stand because his will is firm. Malachi ties Israel's survival to the Lord who does not change—mercy flows from an nature that cannot turn capricious. Believers find stability in a God who is rock-solid in essence, knowledge, purpose, and word.

items.title: Impassibility
items.summary: Impassibility means God is not overcome by suffering or inner turmoil imposed from outside. Modern readers often recoil, fearing a cold deity, yet classic Christianity taught that an unchangeable God can still be fully active, compassionate, and good. Biblical pictures of God's grief or anger speak in human terms; they must not be read as God being swept away like we are. If the divine nature itself suffered eternally, the cross would lose its shock—the immortal willingly entering pain in the flesh. Our comfort is that the Son truly bore our sorrows without collapsing the glory of God.

items.title: Theopaschitism and Patripassianism
items.summary: Ancient churches rejected two errors about suffering on the cross. One claimed the divine nature itself underwent death as God; the other imagined the Father sharing the Son's agony as if they were the same person. Both blur careful distinctions Scripture and creeds guard: the eternal Son assumed a human nature capable of dying, while the Father and Spirit remain distinct persons. Affirming that "God suffered" without qualification risks monophysite or modalist logic. The gospel's wonder is that impassible deity entered real human suffering in the person of Christ, not that suffering defines God's inner life forever.

items.title: Attributes of Intellect
items.summary: Among the traits God shares in measure with rational creatures, those of the mind stand first: knowledge, wisdom, and truthfulness. God's knowing is immediate and exhaustive—nothing learned, nothing hidden, past and future held in one glance. His wisdom directs all events toward ends that display his glory, even when our vantage point is narrow. He is truth itself: unlike idols, incapable of deceit, faithful to covenant promises, and aligned in word and deed. We know in part; he knows archetypally. Trusting his mind is central to Christian hope when life does not add up.

items.title: Attributes of Will
items.summary: God's moral character shines through his will: he is holy, set apart in blazing purity; good in every act; love that gives and sacrifices rather than merely affirming. Grace and mercy meet sinners who deserve otherwise; patience waits while judgment is delayed. Righteousness and justice mean he always does what is right— rewarding good and confronting evil without contradiction. At the cross, love and justice kiss: mercy for the guilty flows through a satisfaction of wrath, so forgiveness is not lawlessness but faithful righteousness. These qualities invite worship and shape how believers treat one another.

items.title: Attributes of Power
items.summary: Omnipotence names God's unmatched ability to accomplish his purposes. Unlike us, he need not struggle with tools or luck; what he wills to do, he can do, often through means but never dependent on them. Sovereignty flows from this power: every star, nation, and heartbeat falls under his governance without canceling creaturely action or responsibility. Many wrestle with that truth, yet power never floats free from God's goodness, wisdom, and faithfulness. The same might that rules galaxies works for the good of those who love him and for the honor of his name.

items.title: Transcendence and Immanence
items.summary: Healthy faith holds two truths together. God is transcendent—high, holy, independent, and incomparably greater than creation. He is also immanent—drawing near, especially in Christ, with personal care. Exalt one without the other and religion warps: pure immanence breeds a tame god; pure transcendence breeds distant fear without fellowship. Isaiah's comfort for exiles weaves both threads: the Creator who never faints also strengthens the weary. God's greatness does not block compassion, and his nearness does not imply weakness. Affliction is not evidence that he is confused or trapped with us, but that the mighty Lord is good enough to help.

items.title: God as Trinity
items.summary: Attributes answer what God is like; the Trinity answers who God is—one divine essence in three eternal persons. This doctrine is not optional decoration for experts but the heartbeat of Christianity, echoed in baptismal formulas and historic creeds. Father, Son, and Spirit are equally God yet personally distinct, deserving equal honor. Though language can feel dense, the truth is meant for devotion: knowing God as he has revealed himself deepens love, not merely curiosity. Practical piety depends on the triune God Jesus unfolded to disciples on the night before the cross.

items.title: The Bible and the Trinity
items.summary: Trinitarian faith can be stated in seven affirmations: one God; Father, Son, and Spirit each fully divine; and none of the persons identical to another. Creeds used careful words not to replace Scripture but to protect these intertwined claims from distortion. Though the word Trinity never appears, the Bible repeatedly presents unified monotheism alongside divine persons— the Father sending, the Son worshiped and equal with God, the Spirit called Lord. Baptismal commands and apostolic blessings name all three together. Orthodoxy arises from many texts read together, inviting believers to understand, teach, and rejoice in triune revelation.

items.title: Trinitarian Terms
items.summary: Centuries of reflection produced precise vocabulary for the mystery of three persons in one God. Notions, properties, relations, and processions describe how Father, Son, and Spirit are known and distinguished without splitting divinity into three gods. The Father is unbegotten and begets the Son; the Son is eternally begotten; the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son in Western confession. One shared substance unites them in glory and power. The terms can dizzy us, but the anchor remains simple: unity of essence, trinity of persons— neither merging the three nor multiplying the one.

items.title: One and Three
items.summary: Classic Trinitarianism confesses three persons of one substance, power, and eternity, distinguished by eternal relations, not by rank or inferior divinity. Orthodoxy rejects shortcuts: Jesus was not merely adopted into godhood at baptism; the Son and Spirit are not impersonal modes of one person; Arian schemes make Christ a lesser being; tritheism treats the Godhead as a committee of separate gods. Healthy doctrine keeps persons distinct while insisting they coinhere in one undivided essence. Gregory of Nazianzus captured the rhythm—think one and immediately see three; distinguish three and return to one—guiding worship toward balanced awe.

items.title: Eternal Generation
items.summary: Eternal generation explains how the Son can be fully God yet not the Father: from eternity the Father communicates divine essence to the Son in an unending, non-physical act. This is not creation in time but personal distinction within one Godhead—begotten, not made. Biblical and creedal language of only Son and God-from-God points here, even when modern translations soften terms. The doctrine guards against both dividing the essence and collapsing the persons. It undergirds hymns that proclaim the incarnate Lord as true deity derived from the Father, worthy of the same worship.

items.title: The Filioque Clause
items.summary: East and West debated whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or also from the Son—the Latin filioque added to the Nicene Creed in the West. Eastern Christians feared unauthorized creedal change and subordination of the Father; Western teachers saw biblical hints that the Spirit is sent by both and called the Spirit of Christ. Reformed voices argued the Father remains the fountain of deity while the Son shares one spiration with him, not two competing sources. The dispute reminds us that pneumatology and Christology stay linked: the Spirit who applies salvation is forever the Spirit of the Son.

items.title: Perichoresis
items.summary: Perichoresis describes mutual indwelling among Father, Son, and Spirit. Each person fully possesses the one divine nature while remaining personally distinct; you cannot encounter one without the others sharing the same undivided being. New Testament language about the Son in the Father and the fullness dwelling in Christ points beyond incarnation alone to eternal fellowship within God. This is not a dance metaphor reducing mystery to movement, nor a blur that merges persons. Coinherence safeguards true threeness and true oneness, grounding worship in a God whose inner life is perfect communion.

items.title: Taxis
items.summary: Trinitarian order—taxis—refers to structured relations, not a ladder of worth. The Father is first as source; the Son receives essence by eternal generation; the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son. Outwardly, creation and redemption unfold from the Father through the Son in the Spirit, never reversed. Statements that the Father is "greater" must be limited to Christ's human mediation, not ontological inferiority of the Son. Persons share one will and equal glory; distinctions describe modes of operation, not competing authorities. Proper order protects both the gospel's sending pattern and the coequality confessed at Nicaea.

items.title: Inseparable Operations
items.summary: The church teaches that outward works of God—creating, saving, sustaining—belong to the whole Trinity, not isolated individuals acting alone. Father, Son, and Spirit share one will and power, so they cannot contradict one another in the world. Yet Scripture still highlights fitting roles: the Son incarnates, the Father sends, the Spirit empowers. Appropriation names which person is especially emphasized without dividing the action. Creation involves word and breath; redemption spans incarnation, cross, and resurrection with all persons active; providence upholds all things through Christ and Spirit. Unity of operation keeps monotheism and personal distinction together.

items.title: Our Triune God and the Christian Life
items.summary: Trinity is not trivia for scholars but fuel for ordinary devotion. Knowing God as three persons is like deepening love for someone dear—joy enough on its own. Creation and new birth are Trinitarian works; the world's unity-in-diversity reflects its Maker. Prayer and worship address Father, through Son, by Spirit. Eternal love among the persons explains generous creation, not lonely need. Relational life among humans mirrors distinction without fusion. Believers may fellowship with each person distinctly—Father as source, Son as advocate and brother, Spirit as comforter—finding safety and delight in the God who is communion itself.

items.title: The Divine Decrees
items.summary: God's decrees are his eternal plan, rooted in his will and character, ordaining what comes to pass for his glory. Though we speak in plural, theologians treat one comprehensive purpose known to God at once, simple like his being, fixed before time, and unchangeable in execution. They are absolute—not conditioned on foreseen human merit—and wise, flowing from counsel rather than whim. God is never the author of sin in the sense of doing evil or being blameworthy, yet even wicked acts fit within a good sovereign design, as Joseph's brothers learned. Trust rests in a purposeful Lord.

items.title: The Will of God
items.summary: Scripture speaks of God's will in more than one sense without dividing God himself. His decretive will is whatever he ordains and infallibly brings to pass—from sparrows falling to history's largest turns. His preceptive will is what he commands and delights in, which rebels may ignore. Believers also talk about discerning personal direction, yet the Bible rarely promises a hidden roadmap for every fork in the road; faith walks step by step. What is clear is the moral will: holiness, Spirit-filled living, fruitfulness, and conformity to Christ. Obedience to revealed commands is the path of wisdom.

items.title: Freedom of the Will
items.summary: After the fall, human choosing is bent toward sin yet still genuinely ours—not forced from outside like a puppet. Medieval and Reformed thinkers sorted kinds of necessity so we can speak honestly: we are not free to love God apart from grace, but our evil acts remain voluntary and blameworthy. God ordains what happens without becoming the doer of wickedness; agents such as Pilate acted freely even when their deeds fit a larger divine plan. Sovereignty does not erase real human willing or erase moral accountability.

items.title: God’s Permission
items.summary: If the Lord works all things according to his plan, we must ask how that relates to sin. Scripture and the Westminster Confession both insist God is not the author of evil, yet his providence is not a passive shrug at wrongdoing. Permission in theology is still purposeful ordering—wise limits and goals—not God looking away. Good and evil are not governed in identical ways, but nothing falls outside his rule. The cross shows how a wicked deed can be within divine purpose while sinners remain guilty.

items.title: Election and Reprobation
items.summary: Election names God's gracious choice of some for eternal life in Christ; predestination often covers the broader eternal ordering of salvation's end and means. Reprobation is the sober counterpart: God passes by some and justly condemns the guilty, not the innocent. These truths are hard yet biblical—vessels of wrath, those appointed to judgment. Reformed teaching distinguishes passing over from punishing so divine justice is not arbitrary. Mystery remains, but the goal is worship: grace displayed to the praise of God's glory.

items.title: Is Predestination Fair?
items.summary: Romans 9 faces head-on whether God is unjust when he shows mercy to some and hardens others. Paul does not rescue the doctrine by making salvation depend on human merit or foreseen faith. Instead he points to who God is: free to show compassion, righteous in displaying his power and holiness through both mercy and judgment. Human fairness is not the measure; Scripture and God's own character are. Election and reprobation serve his glory, including the backdrop against which grace shines.

items.title: The Order of the Decrees
items.summary: Reformed debates about supralapsarianism and infralapsarianism concern logical order in God's eternal plan, not a timeline in heaven. One view places the decree to save some and pass by others before the decree to create and allow the fall; the other places election after creation and fall so mercy addresses guilty sinners. Both aim to honor sovereignty and grace. Dort's language of choosing from a fallen race fits the latter. The issue is worth careful thought but not division where Scripture is silent.

items.title: Amyraldianism
items.summary: After Dort, Moïse Amyraut proposed that Christ died for all people on condition of faith while still holding particular election. That universal intent sat uneasily with classic Reformed order of decrees and the sure efficacy of redemption for the elect. Hypothetical universalism in other thinkers kept unconditional election alongside a conditional offer; Amyraut's sequence risked making God's eternal will depend on what creatures might do. Critics saw Arminian drift. Confessional Reformed churches rejected views that weakened immutable, unconditional decree and definite atonement.

items.title: Middle Knowledge
items.summary: Luis de Molina tried to preserve libertarian freedom and divine control by middle knowledge—God's prevolitional awareness of what free creatures would do in every situation, then choosing a world to match. Reformed critics argue this grants human choice too much independence, leaves counterfactuals oddly grounded, and makes God's will consult creaturely possibilities rather than flow from himself alone. Biblical texts on God's rule over hearts and salvation sit more comfortably with decree before choice. Molinism revises sovereignty and divine self-sufficiency in ways classic Christianity rejects.

items.title: Evangelism and the Sovereignty of God
items.summary: Some claim that if God elects, evangelism becomes pointless. Paul and church history say otherwise. Deep sorrow for the lost and urgent prayer for their salvation lived alongside firm belief in divine mercy and hardening. God told Paul to keep preaching because he had many people in Corinth; missionaries endure hardship for the elect's sake. Calvinistic revivalists and pioneers of modern missions preached widely. The Father draws sinners, yet Christ still calls all who hear to come. Election fuels hope that lost sheep will hear and respond.

items.title: Our Creator God
items.summary: Creation answers who made the cosmos before it answers mechanism or purpose. From Genesis onward, the one true God—not a tribal idol—fashioned heaven, earth, seas, and all hosts, and sustains them. He needs no temple service or human supply; he gives life and breath to all. The world is distinct from God yet wholly dependent on him. There was never a time without the Creator, but there was a time without matter. Knowing him as Maker grounds worship, rejects rival stories, and anchors human place in the universe.

items.title: Creation Ex Nihilo
items.summary: Unlike pagan myths of gods battling primordial chaos, the biblical God speaks the universe into being without preexisting stuff or struggle. Creation out of nothing means absolute dependence on his word, not a rival material or a divine shortage. God and creation are not the same substance—ruling out pantheism, crude dualism, deism, and process views that trap God inside a changing world. Because he transcends what he made, he can enter it lovingly in incarnation rather than merely discovering himself through it.

items.title: Creation Days
items.summary: Evangelicals debate whether Genesis 1's days are twenty-four hours, long ages, a literary framework pairing realms and rulers, or analogical divine workdays. Each view has thoughtful defenders. The author favors ordinary days: evening and morning language, the week's pattern, historic church readings, and Calvin's sense that God accommodated humans in timing as well as wording. That allows a young earth and no animal death before Adam's sin, with mature appearance at creation like Adam's first day. The central claim remains: God personally made a good world by his word.

items.title: Historical Adam
items.summary: Adam was a real man formed by God's direct act, not a mythic symbol divorced from history. Genesis links him seamlessly to Abraham and the rest of Scripture treats him as flesh and blood in genealogies and apostolic teaching. Without one original pair, universal sin, shared dignity, and Paul's parallel between the first man and Christ collapse. Recent proposals of Adam chosen from an existing population struggle with death before the fall, Eve from his side, and one family's guilt. The church's mainstream reading should stand.

items.title: The End for Which God Created the World
items.summary: Creation exists so the living God might be feared, praised, and seen as glorious. He did not make the world because he lacked love or companionship; overflowing goodness and perfection naturally communicate outward like a fountain. Jonathan Edwards captured this: the infinite fullness of divine excellency rightly streams beyond itself. Stars by the billions, microscopic wonder, and human life all invite awe. Christianity begins with a Creator worthy of honor; without that doctrine the gospel loses its foundation. Everything that exists serves to display his worth.

items.title: Angels
items.summary: Angels appear throughout Scripture far more than casual reading suggests. They are created spirits, not divine, with intelligence and personal names though limited power and knowledge. Some fell and remain fixed in rebellion; holy angels guard, message, patrol, and serve God's people and even attended Christ at pivotal moments. Cherubim and seraphim surround God's presence; archangels such as Michael and Gabriel carry major missions. We should neither obsess over angelic speculation nor ignore real heavenly agents. They bridge God's world and ours under his authority.

items.title: Demons
items.summary: Scripture treats evil as personal: Satan and demonic powers oppose God and target believers. Paul lists rulers and spiritual forces in heavenly realms behind darkness on earth—not mere social trends. Pride likely preceded humanity's fall in the angelic rebellion. The devil deceives the nations and accuses God's children, yet Christ rebukes him and secures salvation. Christians need not invent elaborate demon maps or chase every spirit name. Our call is to stand firm in gospel truth, resist, and trust the victory already won at the cross.

items.title: Providence
items.summary: Providence is God's continuous sustaining, accompanying, and directing of all creatures toward his ends. The biblical narrative assumes his hand in big events and small details—from sparrows to kings, from Esther's unseen turns to Joseph's suffering redeemed. He is not the author of sin yet nothing happens apart from his wise purpose, including the crucifixion. Heidelberg Catechism comfort applies: health, hardship, and daily bread come from a fatherly hand, not chance. Sovereignty is not cold fate but the promise that almighty love orders life for those who belong to him.

items.title: Miracles
items.summary: Miracles are God's immediate acts breaking the usual patterns of nature, unlike ordinary providence where he works through means. Biblical signs cluster at redemptive high points—exodus, prophetic ministries, Christ, and the apostles—confirming salvation's message. Defending every odd event today matters less than defending history's central sign: Jesus raised bodily. Ancient hearers found resurrection as unbelievable as modern ones; Paul appealed to public evidence. Christianity rests on supernatural facts—creation, inspired word, virgin birth, incarnation, empty tomb. Deny the miraculous and the faith itself disappears.

items.title: Prayer
items.summary: Prayer belongs to doctrine because God chooses to rule partly through his people's requests. He needs nothing from us yet invites dependence so he receives glory as giver. Calvin urged reverence, sincerity, humility, and confident expectation that the Father hears for Christ's sake—not timid bargaining as if God might be unwilling. Jesus repeatedly commanded asking, seeking, and knocking; neglecting prayer reveals practical atheism. Faith trusts a personal God who moves history through intercession while Christ pleads above. Persistence in prayer is trust wrestling with slow answers.

items.title: Created Being and Crowning Achievement
items.summary: Humans are creatures, not God, yet the height of what he made—crowned with glory and given dominion in Psalm 8 and Genesis 1. Scripture's story centers on people in relation to their Maker, not on earth as an end in itself. That rebuts pictures of humanity as a cancer on pristine nature. We can harm creation but also cultivate beauty, culture, and flourishing as image-bearing stewards. Christians should wisely develop the world for people and praise, not romanticize a human-free wilderness.

items.title: Man as Body and Soul
items.summary: Genesis portrays Adam as dust enlivened by God's breath—a whole person, not merely a body with an optional spiritual add-on. Yet death separates believer from body until resurrection; Paul expects to be with Christ apart from the flesh. Most of church history holds dichotomy—body and soul—over trichotomy, since spirit and soul often parallel in Scripture. The point is pastoral: live for eternal soul-health, not body alone. Modern culture forgets the inner person; biblical faith insists we are more than appetites and appearances.

items.title: Where Do Our Souls Come From?
items.summary: Bodies come from parents through conception; souls have been explained three ways. Preexistence of souls lacks biblical support and downplays embodiment. Traducianism says soul and body both propagate from parents, fitting inherited corruption without God creating evil souls. Creationism holds each soul is directly made by God—common in East, Rome, and much Protestantism—and helps explain how Christ had true humanity without Adam's guilt transmitted through soul generation. Imputation of Adam's sin, not divine manufacture of wickedness, accounts for depravity. Either view keeps body and soul as good gifts needing redemption.

items.title: Faculty Psychology
items.summary: Theologians and philosophers mapped the soul's powers—intellect, will, appetites, senses—much as the body has organs. Aquinas and the wider tradition debated how mind and desire interact; Reformed teaching stresses that fall corrupted every faculty, so reason alone cannot save. Intellect and will dominate Reformed summaries, with careful language distinguishing holy affections from passive passions that sweep us away. Such categories sound abstract yet guard against cold intellectualism and against equating faith with fleeting feelings. Whole-person renewal matters for discipleship.

items.title: Male and Female
items.summary: Humanity is one race yet irreducibly two sexes from creation—male and female bearing God's image together. Scripture highlights appearance, bodily design, characteristic virtues, demeanor, and relational posture: men and women are not interchangeable, confused dress and behavior dishonor nature, bodies signal God's intent, beauty and strength receive distinct emphases, and marriage pictures helper and headship without erasing tenderness or exhortation in both. These patterns extend beyond wedding vows. Sexual difference is deliberate goodness, not cultural accident, to be received not reinvented.

items.title: Marriage
items.summary: Marriage rests on three biblical threads: man and woman fit each other as one flesh reunited from one humanity; covenant loyalty joined to openness to godly children; and the mystery picturing Christ and the church. Complementarity grounds monogamy and exclusivity. Malachi treats marriage as sworn bond whose sexual union ratifies covenant and normally bears offspring—not the only marital good, but built into its design. Ephesians 5 requires distinct husband and wife roles to mirror Savior and bride. Redefining marriage as genderless severs that gospel-shaped symbolism.

items.title: Transgenderism
items.summary: God assigns biological sex as male or female and calls us to live accordingly, regardless of inner turmoil. Creation pairs man and woman for union and fruitfulness; rare intersex conditions illustrate fallen groaning, not a third designed sex. Christians should be compassionate toward deep distress yet refuse the idea that felt identity overrides God's word—same as with other sins rooted in self-rule. Scripture forbids crossing sexual and gender boundaries in behavior and dress. Our bodies belong to the Lord for his glory, not autonomous self-definition.

items.title: Image of God
items.summary: Every person reflects God's image—given at creation, surviving fall and flood, grounding human dignity and the seriousness of murder. New Testament emphasis shifts: Christ perfectly shows the image, and believers are being remade into his likeness from glory to glory. James warns against cursing anyone stamped with that likeness, believer or not. For Christians, image-bearing is present honor and future hope—conformation to the Son for those God foreknew. It defines why human life matters and where redemption is headed.

items.title: What Does It Mean to Be Made in the Image of God?
items.summary: The divine image has been explained in different ways: some stress what humans are built to do—think, choose, worship—while others stress how we are meant to live before God. Scripture especially highlights the calling side of the image. We stand for God in creation, exercising stewardship under his rule. We are made for fellowship with him, able to know and honor our Maker. The image also involves moral likeness—knowledge, holiness, and righteousness—marred by sin but renewed in believers. Only in Christ do we see humanity as it should be; through the gospel and the Spirit, God restores image-bearers into his Son’s likeness.

items.title: What Are the Implications of Being Made in the Image of God?
items.summary: If every person bears God’s image, the consequences reach everywhere. Humans are not merely advanced animals but the crown of creation. That grounds equal dignity: unborn life, the elderly, the disabled, and every ethnicity deserve protection and respect; abortion, racism, and contempt for the vulnerable contradict who we are. True humanity is found in loving and obeying our Creator, not in chasing autonomy. Our presence declares that the world is his, and we ourselves belong to him more deeply than to any earthly power. Worship must center on Christ, the visible image of the invisible God, not on idols of our making.

items.title: The Essence of Sin
items.summary: Sin is active rebellion against God—a condition we inherit and choices we make that lead to death. At root it is lawlessness: failing God’s standard and exchanging him for substitutes, whether outward idols or inward cravings. Scripture uses blunt words—rebellion, treachery, wickedness—because the problem is moral and spiritual, not a polite flaw. Evil first appeared among angels through pride, without external temptation. Adam’s fall mirrored that pattern: doubting God’s word, seeking forbidden pleasure, and acting as if he knew better. Softening sin into mere brokenness hides how serious our guilt is and how desperately we need grace.

items.title: The Origin of Sin
items.summary: Adam’s disobedience in Eden brought death, shame, fear, blame-shifting, pain in relationships, and toil in work. Creation itself was subjected to frustration; thorns, decay, and hardship mark a world under curse. Theologians distinguish the first human sin from “original sin,” the corrupted nature passed to all who descend from Adam, and “actual sin,” the wrongs we willingly commit. Our deepest trouble is not bad upbringing or environment but a heart turned from God from birth. The Bible and experience agree: none is righteous by nature. Hope begins when we admit our uncleanness before the holy King and look for mercy outside ourselves.

items.title: The Transmission of Sin
items.summary: We do not become sinners only by copying bad examples; we enter the world already guilty and corrupt because we were united to Adam. When he broke God’s command, the whole race was counted sinful and subject to death, parallel to how Christ’s obedience brings life to those united to him. Salvation involves three great exchanges: Adam’s guilt credited to us, our guilt borne by Christ, and Christ’s righteousness credited to believers. History turns on two representative heads—the first brought condemnation, the second brings justification. By faith we pass from Adam’s kingdom into the reign of the last Adam and receive eternal life as a gift.

items.title: Total Inability
items.summary: Pelagius taught that people must be able to obey God or blame would be unfair; Augustine answered that the fallen will is enslaved to sin and needs grace even to embrace grace. “Total depravity” means sin touches every faculty, not that everyone is as wicked as possible; “total inability” better captures our helplessness to save or truly reform ourselves. Reformed confessions insist that apart from the Spirit’s regenerating work, no one can turn to God. We are spiritually dead, hostile to God’s law, and unable to come to Christ unless the Father draws us. New birth is entirely God’s work—yet it is our only hope.

items.title: Human Nature in Its Fourfold State
items.summary: Classic Reformed anthropology describes four stages of human existence. In Eden, Adam could obey or fall—he was innocent yet able to sin. After the fall, every natural descendant lives in a state of guilt, misery, and bondage to evil, unable to please God or earn salvation. Those regenerated and united to Christ enter a state of grace: indwelling sin remains, but a new principle of obedience fights within, and believers are servants of righteousness. In glory, the redeemed will be so perfected that sin will be impossible—secure forever in a condition even better than Eden, never again able to turn from God.

items.title: Is Every Sin the Same in God’s Eyes?
items.summary: Because any sin deserves God’s judgment, some conclude all sins are equally serious; others say so to comfort sinners or from humility. Yet Scripture treats offenses differently: the law assigned varied penalties, distinguished deliberate from unintentional wrongs, and judged leaders more strictly than ordinary people. Jesus warned that rejection of clearer light brings heavier condemnation; betrayal of the Son of Man stands apart. God especially opposes harm to the weak. Church discipline, prophetic warnings, and everyday justice all assume degrees of guilt. Eternal punishment for every sin does not mean God sees no difference between careless slip and brazen rebellion.

items.title: Sins Made More Heinous
items.summary: Westminster theology teaches that not every transgression weighs the same; aggravating factors deepen guilt. Who sins matters—teachers, parents, and public Christians face greater accountability. Who is wronged matters—direct offense against God, Christ, the Spirit, authority, or the vulnerable increases severity. The kind of act matters—clear commands, outward deeds, repetition, celebration, and defiance of conscience weigh heavier than gray-area failures. Time and place matter too, especially sin during worship or in the open. Recognizing degrees helps the church speak honestly about public evil, apply warnings and comfort wisely, and pursue holiness without treating every struggle as equal to high-handed rebellion—or excusing serious sin as minor weakness.

items.title: Concupiscence
items.summary: Reformed teaching holds believers accountable for inherited corruption and for sinful desires that arise before any outward act. Even after forgiveness, a bent toward evil remains in the flesh until death. Many disordered longings feel unchosen, which should move us to compassion, yet they still violate God’s law. Roman Catholic teaching often treats such inclination as neutral until the will consents; the Reformers insisted that wrong cravings themselves are sin, part of the depravity Christ’s people war against daily. That honesty is hard but hopeful: what is truly sin can be confessed, mortified, pardoned, and gradually healed by grace.

items.title: Temptation
items.summary: James describes desire conceiving outward sin and sin producing death, but his focus is the path to visible transgression, not a claim that every inner pull is innocent. “Temptation” in Scripture can mean a testing allowed by God or an enticement arising from corrupt desire within. External pressure may be resisted without sin; an evil proposal generated in the heart already reflects indwelling corruption. Christ was genuinely tempted through suffering and Satan’s appeals, yet without sinful longing—he bore temptation’s pain, not its guilt. Believers should resist early: wandering thoughts and entangled affections are not final failure, but they show sin at work and call for vigilance before consent and action.

items.title: What Difference Does the Doctrine of Sin Make?
items.summary: A robust view of sin is not morbid; it shapes wise discipleship. It keeps us realistic about institutions and power—expecting self-interest and designing checks because people fail. It also turns the mirror on us: the problem is not only “them” but our own hearts inclined to hate God and neighbor. That realism fuels mission—the gospel announces rescue for actual sinners, which must stay central in preaching and ministry. And it deepens gratitude: every true believer is a miracle of grace. Knowing how lost we were makes mercy the song of the Christian life, from first conversion to final glory.

items.title: Centrality of Covenant
items.summary: When Jesus explained his death at the Last Supper, he called the cup the blood of the covenant—yet many Christians overlook how central that idea is. “Covenant” appears constantly across Scripture, from creation to consummation, framing God’s dealings with his people and Christ’s priestly work. Covenant theology is a way of reading the whole Bible: triune purpose before time, God’s bond with humanity, and our obligations toward one another. The story of grace unfolds through successive administrations; Christ fulfills what was promised and stands as the second Adam opposite the first. Thoughtful reading from Genesis to Revelation keeps forcing this framework to the surface.

items.title: Definition of Covenant
items.summary: A covenant in Scripture is a solemn agreement in which God binds himself to his people—and often calls them to duty—with promises, commands, and threatened consequences for unfaithfulness. Thinkers have summarized it as a promissory pact between parties, ratified by oaths and signs. Biblical covenants typically include divine pledges, stipulations, penalties, sworn commitments, witnesses, written words, and ceremonial seals. Not every element appears every time, but the pattern repeats: God initiates, defines terms, and marks the relationship publicly. From Noah to Christ, the Lord relates to creatures through these structured promises rather than vague sentiment, which is why covenant language is essential to understanding redemption.

items.title: Berith and Diatheke
items.summary: Hebrew berith and Greek diatheke both point to covenant, though older interpreters sometimes heard “testament” in the New Testament, especially in Hebrews. Some verses mention death activating an arrangement, which sounds like a will; yet context often fits covenant ceremonies—slain animals, self-curses, blood sealing the bond—better than modern inheritance law. Recent scholarship suggests Greek “testaments” did not require the testator’s death to distribute goods. Even where testament imagery appears, covenant and will differ: covenants invoke death at the beginning as oath and sacrifice; testaments assume death at the end. Christ interpreted his cross as covenant blood for rebels, fulfilling what berith always meant.

items.title: Worship as Covenant Renewal
items.summary: Exodus 24 portrays Israel confirming God’s bond at Sinai in a gathering that doubles as a worship pattern for generations. Leaders and people draw near; Moses proclaims God’s words and written stipulations; the nation twice pledges obedience. Sacrifice and sprinkled blood mark substitution, atonement, and consecration—covenant life bought and sealed in blood. Elders eat and drink in God’s presence, signifying fellowship secured by the sacrifice. That service includes call, approach through blood, reading, response, meal, and nearness of God—the same rhythm Christian assemblies echo when they hear the Word, trust Christ’s sacrifice, and celebrate the Lord’s Supper as covenant remembrance.

items.title: Covenant of Redemption
items.summary: Before creation, the Father and Son agreed to save a people chosen in Christ—the eternal covenant of redemption. It explains how election, history, and Trinitarian love fit together and gives believers confidence that their salvation rests on a pact older than the world. Critics say it sidelines the Spirit, splits God’s will, or lacks biblical warrant. Reformed teachers reply that the Spirit applies what the Son earns; Father and Son share one divine purpose viewed from different roles; and Scripture presents the Son sent to do the Father’s will, promised a people, enthroned as king, and bringing peace as the covenant head. Grace in time flows from that prior agreement.

items.title: Covenant of Works
items.summary: The covenant of works names God’s arrangement with Adam as representative of humanity: perfect obedience would bring life; eating the forbidden fruit brought death for himself and the race. Other labels emphasize Eden, creation, or promised life, but “works” highlights that blessing depended on Adam’s fulfillment, not unmerited favor. Some deny the label because Genesis never says “covenant” or because they see only divine kindness. Yet garden elements mirror later covenants—command, promise, penalty, oath, witnesses, and the tree of life—and Hosea compares Israel’s treachery to Adam’s breaking of covenant. Paul pairs Adam and Christ as parallel heads; if Christ’s saving work is covenantal, Adam’s fatal failure must be too.

items.title: Covenant of Grace
items.summary: After Adam’s fall, humans cannot keep the original standard of works. God establishes the covenant of grace, offering life and salvation through Christ to undeserving sinners who receive it by faith—which itself is his gift. Entrance is free, yet believing obedience marks those who enjoy covenant blessings. Throughout history some belong outwardly without true heart faith, as circumcised infants could lack inward renewal; the same possibility exists where people are visibly in the church but reject the Savior. Administrations change from Abraham to Moses to the present age, but one gracious promise runs through all: God will be our God and we his people, fulfilled most clearly in Christ.

items.title: The Noahic Covenant
items.summary: After the flood, God pledged to preserve the world: seasons would continue, and he would not again destroy the earth with water. The rainbow serves as a sign—for humanity and as a reminder even to God—of that patience. Unlike later redemptive seals, this covenant is bloodless and universal, made with Noah’s family, all descendants, and living creatures. It is chiefly common grace, sustaining a fallen world so special grace can unfold, not replacing the saving covenant but upholding creation. God restates human dignity, fruitfulness, and dominion, assuming sin’s reality while delaying global judgment until the final fire. The bow in the clouds points to restrained wrath and ongoing opportunity for gospel work.

items.title: Abrahamic Covenant
items.summary: God chose Abram from an idolatrous household—not because he deserved it—and promised personal blessing, a great nation, and worldwide good through his offspring, which the New Testament calls gospel announcement. Threats to the promise repeatedly appeared, yet Abraham trusted God, was counted righteous, and saw the covenant ratified in a solemn ceremony. Later, circumcision marked Abraham’s line as set apart, pointing to heart renewal for the faithful and judgment for the rebellious. The near-sacrifice of Isaac tested and displayed trust, while highlighting divine provision. That covenant becomes a anchor throughout Scripture, culminating in the son of Abraham who blesses every nation through faith.

items.title: Mosaic Covenant
items.summary: At Sinai God bound Israel to blessings for obedience and curses for persistent rebellion, yet the sacrificial system shows the Mosaic era as an administration of grace, not a second path of earning heaven by merit. It advanced redemption with national scope, vivid types of holiness, and laws exposing sin. Compared with the new covenant, its glory was dimmer, like a furnished room awaiting brighter light. Conditions under Moses differed from Eden: failure could be atoned, exile followed impenitence, not a single bite of fruit. The law instructs, restrains, and guides grateful believers; it was never meant to cancel the promise to Abraham but to teach a redeemed people how to live before God.

items.title: Republication
items.summary: Some Reformed teachers argue the Mosaic covenant “republished” Adam’s works principle—especially through commands like “do them and live”—so Israel, as a typological Adam, could be exiled for covenant failure, and Paul contrasts law with promise sharply. Others reply that Paul addresses opponents who misuse the law for self-justification, not Moses’s full teaching, which aligns with gospel. Theologically, grace and works covenants operate on different principles; mixing them risks confusing how obedience relates to salvation. Classic distinctions say works were required in Eden to earn life, whereas under Moses good works follow justification as fruit. How one reads Leviticus 18:5 therefore shapes covenant theology and the Christian use of God’s moral law.

items.title: Davidic Covenant
items.summary: When David’s kingdom rested and the ark sat in Jerusalem, God promised an enduring dynasty, a great name, rest, and a son on the throne treated as his own royal child. Though the word covenant is absent in the narrative, Psalms and later texts apply it clearly. Promises to Abraham and Moses find focus in a king who would embody Israel before God. Near fulfillment shone in Solomon’s reign but faded through sin; ultimate fulfillment awaits a greater Son who reigns forever. Expectation of a Davidic Messiah shaped Jewish hope and the Gospels, which present Jesus as that promised king through whom salvation comes.

items.title: New Covenant
items.summary: Jeremiah foretold a new covenant unlike the broken Mosaic bond yet built from earlier promises: forgiven sin, God’s law on the heart, and knowing the Lord personally. “New” mainly contrasts with Sinai’s failure, not with Abraham’s grace. The covenant remains corporate—made with Israel and Judah—while touching each believer inwardly. In Christ and the Spirit many blessings are already present: access to God, internal transformation, and pardon. Full realization awaits glory, when knowledge will be complete and mediation unnecessary. The new covenant completes what the covenant of grace always aimed at, intensifying inner renewal, assurance, and communion without abolishing the one people of God.

items.title: The Fathers Have Eaten Sour Grapes
items.summary: Exiles quoted a proverb blaming ancestors for their pain; Jeremiah and Ezekiel reject that excuse. God had warned that sin’s effects ripple through families, yet blessing and judgment still relate to how each generation responds to him. Mosaic law already forbade executing children for fathers’ crimes. Throughout Israel’s story, righteous remnants often escaped corporate judgment. The prophets’ point is not that the old covenant punished innocents for others’ guilt, but that Judah truly deserved exile for its own rebellion. New-covenant hope includes forgiveness and transformed hearts so God’s people stop shifting blame and start walking in renewed obedience before him.

items.title: The Newness of the New Covenant
items.summary: God’s promise in Christ both continues and advances what came before. Like earlier eras, people can share in the outward community of the covenant yet reject its heart by despising Christ’s sacrifice. Still, what Christ brings is genuinely new: clearer revelation, fuller grace, freedom as adopted children, blessing for every nation, and a covenant that never ends. Hebrews shows Moses was faithful, but Jesus mediates a superior arrangement. The ceremonial law tied to Moses has fulfilled its purpose; the covenant rooted in Christ is fresh, second, better, and everlasting.

items.title: The Law and the Christian
items.summary: Believers are not freed from obedience but from the law’s curse. Christ ends the law as a way to earn righteousness, yet God’s commands remain holy and must be used rightly. Jesus did not discard the Old Testament; he brought it to its intended goal. Food laws, temple rituals, and national statutes have shifted with his coming, but moral wisdom and the law’s witness to Christ still guide us. Paul even applies Moses’ instructions to church life, showing Scripture is reinterpreted through the Messiah, not thrown away.

items.title: Threefold Division of the Law
items.summary: Reformed Christians often sort Moses’ law into moral, ceremonial, and civil parts. Critics say the Bible never labels them that way, but church history and Scripture itself support a real distinction. The Ten Commandments stand apart: spoken directly by God, written in stone, and binding on the conscience before Sinai. Other statutes functioned as case law, with worship regulations pointing to something greater and land-specific rules tied to Israel’s nationhood. Moses’ people never treated every command as equal; neither should we when applying the law today.

items.title: Dispensationalism
items.summary: Dispensationalism reads the Bible as sharply separating national Israel from the church and often takes prophetic details in a very literal way. It grew from John Nelson Darby and spread widely through study Bibles that mapped history into distinct eras of testing and mercy. Later forms softened some distinctive teachings while still emphasizing future earthly promises for ethnic Israel. Covenant theology, by contrast, stresses one people of God united in Christ. Gentile believers are grafted in, not sidelined, and the church shares in the blessings promised to Abraham’s true offspring.

items.title: Baptist Covenant Theology
items.summary: Baptists have their own rich covenant tradition, seen in confessions that echo Westminster Calvinism while differing on church and sacraments. Classic Baptist theology says earlier covenants reveal the one covenant of grace but only the new covenant actually administers its blessings in union with Christ. Some recent Baptist thinkers seek a middle path between dispensationalism and Presbyterian covenant theology, stressing one storyline of covenants without the classic works-grace pairing or binding status of the Decalogue as moral law. Reformed believers still debate how radically new the new covenant is for community, baptism, and membership.

items.title: The Israel of God
items.summary: God’s ancient choice of Israel still matters, but identity as God’s people now turns on faith in Jesus. Reformed teaching is not about replacing Jews with Gentiles but reconstituting Israel around its Messiah. Jesus redefined belonging: follow him and you are part of his renewed people, signaled by twelve apostles and his bold claims to be the true bread, light, and door. New Testament writers apply Israel’s titles—chosen nation, royal priesthood, treasured possession—to the multinational church. True Israel is wherever people trust and obey the God who came in Christ.

items.title: Logos
items.summary: John opens his Gospel by echoing Genesis: before creation there was the Word, eternally with God and fully God, through whom all things were made. The Word is not a lesser being or the first creature but shares the Father’s divine nature while remaining distinct from him. Grammar and context reject translations that downgrade Christ to “a god.” John balances full deity against the Father with real personal distinction, guarding against both denying Christ’s godhood and collapsing Father and Son into one person. The prologue leads to worship: the risen Jesus is Lord and God.

items.title: Virgin Birth
items.summary: Matthew and Luke teach plainly that Mary conceived Jesus as a virgin through the Holy Spirit’s work. Skeptics challenge the Isaiah prophecy’s wording or claim pagan copycats, but Hebrew and Greek usage support a virgin, Jewish culture would not invent pagan myths, and alleged parallels are weak or late. From the early church onward, Christians have insisted on this truth because it secures both Christ’s full humanity and his freedom from Adam’s sinful line. The Spirit’s role in his conception fits the gospel: our Savior is truly one of us, yet without sin.

items.title: Messianic Prophecies
items.summary: Long before Bethlehem, Scripture pointed forward to a deliverer from Abraham’s line, David’s house, and Judah’s tribe—a king, prophet, and suffering servant. Matthew especially presents Jesus as Israel’s story retold faithfully: escape from a murderous king, passage through water, wilderness testing, and finally the Father’s approval where the nation failed. Prophetic texts were not ripped from context; the evangelists saw Christ completing patterns Israel only shadowed. Jesus is the Son who obeyed where the old covenant people rebelled, bearing their story to its saving climax.

items.title: Names and Titles of Jesus
items.summary: The name Jesus means the Lord saves—a common Jewish name filled with cosmic meaning. The New Testament piles titles on him: Word, Immanuel, Lamb, bread, King, image of God, high priest, Alpha and Omega, and more. Five stand out. Christ marks him as God’s anointed King. Son of God speaks of unique relationship and shared glory with the Father. Son of Man draws on Daniel’s vision of one who approaches the Ancient of Days. Lord confesses his rule over all. Explicit statements call him God—titles reserved for the one we worship.

items.title: Jesus’s Witness to Himself
items.summary: To know Christ, listen to how he spoke about himself, especially in John. He claimed to be heaven’s bread, the world’s light, the sheep’s gate, the good shepherd, resurrection and life, the only way to the Father, and the vine we must abide in. Without him, people hunger, wander in darkness, and face judgment. He also used stark “I am” declarations that recall God’s name to Moses, showing eternal self-existence. Jesus placed himself alongside the Father as an object of trust. His own words leave no neutral ground about who he is.

items.title: Autotheos
items.summary: In John 5 Jesus insists that dishonoring him dishonors the Father, because he does whatever the Father does, shares the Father’s life-giving power, and holds authority to judge. The Son possesses life in himself—the self-existence proper to God—not as a secondary deity granted divinity from above. Reformed teachers say he is God in his own right as to essence, even while his person eternally comes from the Father. We meet the true God only through this Son, who deserves the same honor due the Father and can raise the dead because he is the living God.

items.title: Deity of Christ
items.summary: Scripture presents Jesus as more than a great teacher. He existed before creation, received grace for believers before time began, and displays every attribute of God—holiness, authority, eternity, unchangeableness, omnipresence, omnipotence, and omniscience. He rules all things, sits on God’s throne, creates and sustains the universe, and will judge the world. People worship him without rebuke, though worship belongs to God alone. The New Testament’s cumulative witness is clear: the man from Nazareth is the eternal Son, God with us in flesh.

items.title: Humanity of Christ
items.summary: Jesus was not a phantom or angel in disguise. He had a real body, grew up in a family, learned, aged, grew hungry and tired, wept, bled, and died. Emotionally he knew anguish, anger, compassion, and sorrow. He faced temptation yet remained sinless—the last Adam who is as truly human as the first. The Son became man so he could die for everyone, destroy the devil’s hold through death, and serve as a merciful high priest who atones for sin. God took flesh so death would lose its grip on those he came to save.

items.title: Eternal Sonship
items.summary: Ancient Arian teaching claimed the Son had a beginning: divine in a sense, yet created and not sharing the Father’s essence. Biblical faith answers that there never was a time when the Son was not. Jesus identifies himself with Yahweh’s eternal “I am,” shares Isaiah’s exclusive divine claims in Philippians, and in Revelation bears the titles of the everlasting God. If the Son were not eternal, the Father would not always have been Father, and we would lack a Savior who is fully God. Eternal sonship guards both Trinity and salvation.

items.title: Incarnation
items.summary: The incarnation means the eternal Son took a true human nature and lived as Jesus Christ. Only the Son could do this: the Father sends, the Spirit empowers, but the person who became man is the second person of the Trinity. God’s essence did not morph into flesh; the Son assumed humanity without ceasing to be God. He added what he was not while remaining what he always was. The God-man is divine life joined to Mary’s offspring—a new personal existence beginning at conception, while the Logos himself had no beginning.

items.title: Hypostatic Union
items.summary: Orthodox Christology confesses one Savior in two complete natures—divine and human—united in a single person. Christ has one “I,” not two competing selves. The union is personal, not a conversation between natures like the Trinity’s fellowship. Technical terms stress that he did not unite with a separate human person named Jesus apart from the Logos; rather, the human nature subsists only in the Son. His humanity was never a free-floating human individual but always the humanity of God’s Son from the moment of the virgin conception.

items.title: Communicatio Idiomatum
items.summary: Because Christ is one person with two natures, Scripture speaks boldly: what belongs to either nature can be said of him as a whole. He slept in the boat; he also created the world. We must not assign every action to both natures—divinity does not nap, humanity did not speak galaxies into being. Yet we may praise “God’s blood” or say God died on the cross when we mean the incarnate Son, not the Father or the bare divine essence.
